newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bidders submit Thomson privatization offers.
newsitem.headline: Bidders submit Thomson privatization offers.

text.p: France's Alcatel Alsthom and Lagardere Groupe on Monday both submitted their bids to the government to acquire electronics and defence company Thomson SA, a Finance Ministry spokesman said.
The government is expected to decide at the end of this month or early October which of the two companies will get the green light.

Alcatel, the industrial conglomerate headed by Serge Tchuruk, has conducted a silent campaign to win backers in the government for its offer to buy all of Thomson, both the money-losing Thomson Multimedia consumer electronics arm as well as the 58 percent-owned Thomson-CSF defence electronics company.

Lagardere, in contrast, has been waging a more public campaign for its offer, which foresees it obtaining at least a 60 percent stake. Lagardere, which owns Matra, is mainly interested in the defence electronics activities, together with its ally, British Aerospace Plc.

Korea's Daewoo Electronics would obtain control over the multimedia activities, which include such brands as Saba and RCA. Daewoo's president Bae Soon Hoon told the Les Echos newspaper Monday that he aimed to make the activities profitable within two years.

Noel Forgeard, the chairman of Lagardere's defence and space activities, said that the assets of Matra would be transferred to Thomson-CSF to create Thomson-Matra, which would remain listed on the Paris Bourse. BA could hold 5 percent in Thomson-Matra and Thomson employees between 5 percent and 6 percent.

For the government, and President Jacques Chirac, there are a number of key questions that will decide who will win. Neither of the two bids will raise much money for the state due to the multimedia losses -- incurred because of heavy investments in new technologies at a time of rapid market changes.

Thomson Multimedia lost 3 billion francs ($581 million) in the first half of 1996 and is reported to be planning a restructuring that would include the elimination of 5,000 jobs out of a work force of 49,500, mainly outside France.

Thomson SA Chairman Marcel Roulet will want to make sure the future of the company is assured and that a takeover bid makes industrial sense. With French unemployment standing at over 12 percent, the goverment is unlikely to favour a plan which foresees big job losses in the near future.
